args.text:
1. Read the rules and my secret values and contract before any offer.
2. Trade only when the deal moves me toward my contract or raises my value total.
3. Never give away goods I need; keep to promises exactly and on time.
4. Prefer offers that are clear and specific; decline vague deals.
5. Check each counterparty's holdings before accepting; the bank refuses unfunded trades.
6. Use escrow for future deliveries when a shipment is not yet in hand.
7. Keep messages short; they bind nobody, so verify with the bank's book.
8. After each game, note which trades paid off and which prices were fair.

The bank is the only way goods move. offer: to one trader or to all, what you give now and what you want now, and optionally goods you deliver later (by the end of a later round): either held in escrow by the bank (it takes them at the trade, or reserves them from your shipment if it arrives by then, and delivers them; fee 1 salt) or as a plain promise that you keep with give (the bank tells everyone whether it was kept). accept executes an offer only if both sides hold what it moves; decline or withdraw close it; an offer lasts until the end of the round after the one it was made in; you may have 3 open offers at once. At the end of every round but the last, one perishable good (announced when the round starts) spoils: every trader holding 2 or more units of it loses one, and a quarter (rounded down) of a stock of 8 or more; a single unit keeps. text:
I'm working out why the contract failed: the goods I needed were scarce and everyone was hoarding them for their own contracts. I also waited too long and offered too little salt early, and salt was plentiful and worth little to others, so those trades went nowhere. Next time I'd count supply against demand across all four contracts in round one, and if the goods I need are held by others, I'd pivot right away.

I'm drafting the lessons as a numbered list: check supply against demand across all four contracts in round one, offer goods that contract-holders actually need early instead of salt, use spare goods as trade currency, and accept salt-for-cloth-type offers late when I value the good less than salt. I'm also keeping the rule not to withdraw early offers without replacement, and noting that my score this game was 29.

The game: a market of 4 traders and five goods (salt, cloth, copper, spice, wax), 6 trading rounds long. Every trader starts with 6 salt and a bundle of the other goods; part of its goods comes later, as one shipment at the end of a named round. A trade that moves more than 6 units now costs each side 1 salt of tax. give hands goods over for nothing back. say sends a short message to everyone or to one trader (3 per round). The game: a market of 4 traders and five goods (salt, cloth, copper, spice, wax), 6 trading rounds long. Every trader starts with 6 salt and a bundle of the other goods; part of its goods comes later, as one shipment at the end of a named round. Each unit you hold at the end is worth points to you: salt 2 points for everyone; cloth, copper, spice and wax 1 to 4 points, a different secret value for each trader. Each trader also has a secret contract: a bundle of three goods; if you hold at least that bundle when the game ends, you get 20 more points. The goods you need sit mostly with the others, so you will have to trade. Holdings and shipments are public (the bank's book is open); values and contracts stay secret until the game ends, so what others say about theirs may be true or not. The bank is the only way goods move. offer: to one trader or to all, what you give now and what you want now, and optionally goods you deliver later (by the end of a later round): either held in escrow by the bank (it takes them at the trade, or reserves them from your shipment if it arrives by then, and delivers them; fee 1 salt) or as a plain promise that you keep with give (the bank tells everyone whether it was kept). accept executes an offer only if both sides hold what it moves; decline or withdraw close it; an offer lasts until the end of the round after the one it was made in; you may have 3 open offers at once. A trade that moves more than 6 units now costs each side 1 salt of tax. give hands goods over for nothing back. say sends a short message to everyone or to one trader (3 per round). At the end of every round but the last, one perishable good (announced when the round starts) spoils: every trader holding 2 or more units of it loses one, and a quarter (rounded down) of a stock of 8 or more; a single unit keeps. The match has 4 games; your points from all games add up. The deals rotate: every 4 games use the same 4 positions (goods, values, contract, shipment), passed on one seat each game, so every trader plays every position once.
